The government provides shared infrastructure services to government agencies through ARSAT, which owns a medium-sized data center. As data use and digital government services expand, ARSAT will need to expand its capacity to meet increased demand and provide new and more secure cloud computing, hosting, and housing services, which are expected to lead to cost savings for the Government in the medium term. Cloud migration has led to up to 80 percent in cost savings related to IT infrastructure maintenance in some developed countries. Data centers and computing capacities are essential inputs for the public sector to leverage Artificial Intelligence (AI), big data analytics and other data-related technologies that are increasingly implemented in the management and delivery of public services. Additionally, the local data infrastructure is increasingly vulnerable to climate-related events, as the effects of climate change risks affecting the AMBA area have become more severe, especially through increasing flooding, heatwaves, and extreme precipitation events. These risks have the potential to damage the elements required for those data centers to perform, such as cooling systems, and need to be upgraded to ensure their resilience. Under this projected scenario, it is necessary to ensure all data infrastructure can withstand these events and that proper measures are in place to ensure increased climate resilience and continuity of key digital services.

The FTTP network deployed under Subcomponent 1.1 will provide the infrastructure layer that will be used under this subcomponent 1.2 to connect government agencies and establish secure cross- government data and information exchange at the national level. Finally, this subcomponent will also support expanded public access by financing the installation of public Wi-Fi hotspots in rural areas.

The Government has adopted a government-wide approach to data infrastructure and is consolidating all government server rooms and Network Operations Centers (NOCs) into a standardized government cloud infrastructure. Congo is currently connected to only one submarine cable (West Africa Cable System (WACS16), with a landing station in Pointe-Noire, exclusively managed by the state- owned incumbent operator Congo Telecom (CT). Due to the current instable international connectivity (several outages occurred in 2020 and amid the presidential election in March 2021) and increased demand, there is an urgent need for diversification. Redundancy via terrestrial fiber optic links (currently owned by the GoC) remains limited. CT has an interconnection with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) since 2017 (10GB-capacity linking Brazzaville to Kinshasa through a sub-river cable) and Liquid Telecom, a leading private telecommunication operator in Africa, inaugurated a 20GB-capacity wireless link across the Congo River between Congo and DRC in September 2021. The interconnection with Gabon established under the World Bank-financed Central African Backbone (CAB) regional project (P122398) is operated and commercialized by Mambs Services (a Congolese private sector company) under a seven-year contract. Under the CAB Project, financed by the African Development Bank (AfDB), Congo should also interconnect with Cameroon and the Central African Republic. Due to COVID-19, the project has faced delays and is now expected to be completed by the end of 2022. Additionally, Meta-backed (previously Facebook) submarine cable project, 2Africa, plans to install a submarine cable landing station in Pointe-Noire by the end of 2022. The arrival of the new landing station cable is expected to help reduce prices and contribute to strong growth in broadband subscription.

47. The blend of underground and aerial infrastructure for terrestrial fiber optic infrastructure will be determined during the final technical design and specification of the bidding documents. Aerial infrastructure capital expenditures (CAPEX) costs are almost two times lower and OPEX costs are slightly lower compared to underground infrastructure. However, aerial infrastructure is more vulnerable to natural disasters. Natural disasters such as typhoons occur regularly in FSM. With 8,400 mm of precipitation per year, Pohnpei is also one of the wettest regions in the world. This climate can damage an aerial network. If a disaster happens, aerial infrastructure may be damaged leading to outages and significant replacement costs. However, underground infrastructure faces other risks as well. Uncontrolled digging can damage the cables while people will be careful to stay away from the aerial cables since they would be adjacent to the power lines. Repair of underground infrastructure is more costly and more time- consuming. Flooding is also a particular threat to underground fiber infrastructure. It is assumed that the core fiber on each of the main islands (Pohnpei, Yap and Kosrae) will be buried underground. The periphery of the networks, including drops to individual premises, will be aerial utilizing existing infrastructure, particularly existing poles for electricity distribution. The cost of the fiber drops to individual premises is a relatively small proportion of total costs, comprising approximately US$1.1M of the US$8.8M total needed to install the on-island fiber infrastructure.

This activity will finance to enable data-driven climate adaptation measures at various stages of the climate early-warning communication value chain, focusing on early warning system (EWS) communication infrastructure deployment, early warning information generation, and last-mile information dissemination. And for effective last-mile information dissemination, the project will finance the inclusion of weather information as one of the services to be available under the Government Service Platform (GSP). Weather information from the meteorological system will be interfaced with the GSP and formatted to be available as user-friendly messages sent to citizens through text messages (for example, Unstructured Supplementary Service Data [USSD]), voice-based services (such as Interactive Voice Response (IVR)), and mobile and Web-based interfaces like WhatsApp and Facebook Messenger.

10. Single Sign-on Digital Identifier Platform. The facility for digital identification of users constitutes the backbone for the provision of e-government services as they allow safe, secure and legally verifiable access to these services. This facility creates the legal foundations for the validation of contractual and non-contractual interactions between the government and citizens. Digital identification allows governments to move services online, resulting in improvements in efficiency, productivity, and user satisfaction. In a post-disaster situation, this facility is critical to facilitate the transactions to which citizens typically need access (e.g. social transfers and citizen records such as deeds and birth certificates). Aerial infrastructure capital expenditures (CAPEX) costs are almost two times lower and OPEX costs are slightly lower compared to underground infrastructure. However, aerial infrastructure is more vulnerable to natural disasters. Natural disasters such as typhoons occur regularly in FSM. With 8,400 mm of precipitation per year, Pohnpei is also one of the wettest regions in the world. This climate can damage an aerial network. If a disaster happens, aerial infrastructure may be damaged leading to outages and significant replacement costs. However, underground infrastructure faces other risks as well. Uncontrolled digging can damage the cables while people will be careful to stay away from the aerial cables since they would be adjacent to the power lines. Repair of underground infrastructure is more costly and more time- consuming. Flooding is also a particular threat to underground fiber infrastructure. It is assumed that the core fiber on each of the main islands (Pohnpei, Yap and Kosrae) will be buried underground. The periphery of the networks, including drops to individual premises, will be aerial utilizing existing infrastructure, particularly existing poles for electricity distribution. 13. Legal framework for cybersecurity. Nigeria has a Cybercrime Act (2015) which aimed to also cover issues related to cybersecurity. However, a legislative review, conducted in 2018, found that this combined legislation does not provide for sufficient treatment of cybersecurity and recommended that Nigeria consider maintaining separate laws for each of these areas. It further recommended that amended cybersecurity legislation should clearly state the penalties for breaches of obligations by CNII holders rather than empowering the respective sectorial regulators—not all of which are yet in place—to define the penalties for cybersecurity breaches in their sector and potentially cause misalignment of penalties across sectors. An amended law should also define the time line for the reporting of cybersecurity incidents, contain provisions for requiring cybersecurity service providers and products to be licensed, and establish clear powers of the national CERT to prevent and investigate cybersecurity breaches. The amended cybersecurity legal framework should also set standards for IT security of government information systems and databases.
